title: Retention: CRM & customer lifetime value
source: Session 8 handout (DDM 25/26) – Lilien et al. (2017), Mittal et al. (2023), HBR (2010), MadCool examples, Maru Batting Centre case
tagline: Winning a customer is expensive; keeping a valuable one pays. CRM shifts the focus from single transactions to the lifetime value of each typical customer – measured with retention, survival and CLV.
goals: explain why **CRM** gains importance and what questions a value-based approach answers
compute **market share, sales growth, acquisition rate and acquisition cost**
compute **retention, survival rate and average lifetime**
compute **CLV** and compare segments by it

blocks.title: Trends that make CRM important
head: Trend
Behind it
CRM relevance
rows: Slow population growth, mature markets; ads more expensive and less effective
Shift from acquisition to maximising the value of existing customers: loyalty, upselling, retention
Growth depends on nurturing existing customers; trust beats one-off promotions
Lifecycle marketing, nurturing leads, long-term value instead of transactions
Young, digital consumers experiment; switching is cheap and easy online
Monitor engagement, spot churn signals, targeted retention

items.text: The practice of analysing and using marketing databases and communication technologies to determine practices that **maximise the lifetime value of each (typical) customer** – “typical” = representative of a segment.
A deeply held commitment to re-buy or re-patronise a preferred product in the future despite situational influences and marketing efforts that could cause switching (HBR, 2010).
The **present value of the future (net) cash flows** associated with a particular customer – forward-looking, predictive rather than precise, calculated differently in different settings.

blocks.title: Questions a customer-value approach answers
items: What is the expected future value of a customer or segment – and who are the most valuable ones?
How can we acquire more high-value customers and retain the best ones?
Why do customers churn and how can we prevent it?
How should we allocate marketing resources across segments?

sections.heading: CLV analytics: the metrics
sections.lead: All metrics are empirical – they come from your own records and market reports.

blocks.name: Market share
vars: s_{j} = sales of the focal firm (internal records)
Σ s_{i} = category sales of all firms (market reports, competitive intelligence)

blocks.name: Acquisition rate and cost
blocks.formula: Acq. rate (%) = 100 × prospects acquired / prospects targeted     Acq. cost = acquisition spending / prospects acquired

blocks.title: MadCool Festival
given: Target market 200,000 people; 60,000 tickets sold by March
blocks.result: MS 33.3 % · growth 20 % · acquisition rate 30 % · €50 per acquired customer

blocks.title: Customer activity metrics
head: Metric
Meaning
rows: Share of customers buying in t, given they bought in t−1
Share of those who bought in t−1 but not in t = 1 − Rr
Share of a cohort still active in t since the start of observation
How long a customer stays with the firm

blocks.name: Retention rate
blocks.formula: Rr_{t} (%) = 100 × customers of the cohort buying in t / customers of the cohort buying in t−1

blocks.name: Average lifetime (constant retention)
blocks.note: Lifetime 4 years → Rr = 1 − 1/4 = **75 %**. Lifetime 1 year → Rr = 0 %. Rr = 90 % → lifetime 10 periods.

blocks.name: Survival rate
blocks.formula: SR_{t} = Rr_{t} × SR_{t−1}     with SR_{1} = Rr_{1}
blocks.note: Retention describes one period; survival summarises how many of the original cohort are left.

blocks.title: MadCool: survival of a cohort of 1,000
blocks.result: After four periods only about 17 % of the cohort survive – even though retention rises every period.

blocks.title: Retention vs. survival of the MadCool cohort
blocks.caption: Survival can only fall: it multiplies the retention rates of all periods so far.

blocks.name: Average lifetime duration from cohort data
blocks.formula: Avg. lifetime = Σ_{t=1}^{T} (t × number of customers retained in t) / N

blocks.name: CLV (simple version used in class)
blocks.formula: CLV = lifetime revenues (or margins) − acquisition costs (per client)
vars: Lifetime revenues = order value × purchase frequency × lifetime
Lifetime unknown but Rr constant → lifetime = 1 / (1 − Rr)
blocks.note: Correct CLV tells you what a customer is worth, estimates customer equity, segments by value, sharpens targeting and balances retention vs. acquisition spending. With discounting (Maru case): sum the present values of yearly profits.

blocks.title: One client – with known lifetime or with retention rate
given: Order value 10 € · 12 purchases per year · acquisition cost 200 €
(a) lifetime 10 years · (b) lifetime unknown, constant Rr = 90 %

blocks.title: Polkaly – which segment by CLV? (20 % overhead)
blocks.result: Education has the highest CLV (10,500) – the small, slow-growing segment is the most valuable per client.

blocks.title: E-commerce segments over three months (exam 2019/20)
given: Monthly margin = margin per transaction × frequency
Monthly profit = monthly margin × survival rate (− CAC in month 1)
blocks.result: Segment B (1,920) beats A (622): much higher retention outweighs its double acquisition cost.

blocks.title: Maru Batting Centre (case logic)
blocks.text: For each segment: **CAC** (ad cost / customers won, list + event cost / response), **break-even** = CAC / yearly profit (without discounting), then **CLV** with discounted yearly profits until the yearly NPV falls below ¥100. Judge promotions (discounts, free bats, a second ward) by whether the gain in retention or response raises CLV − CAC more than it costs.

recap: CRM maximises the **lifetime value of each typical customer**; acquisition is getting more expensive and loyalty weaker.
Chain: satisfaction → retention, WOM, spending → firm performance.
**MS** = own sales / market sales; **growth** = Δsales / last period; **acquisition rate** = acquired / targeted; **acquisition cost** = spend / acquired.
**Rr** = buyers in t / buyers in t−1; attrition = 1 − Rr; **lifetime = 1 / (1 − Rr)**.
**CLV = lifetime revenues/margins − acquisition costs**; compare segments per client, include overhead if given.
exam: Fill-the-gaps table (retention, survival, monthly profit, cumulative profit) for two segments and choose one.
CLV per segment from revenue, lifetime and CAC (Polkaly) – often combined with the conjoint part of the mini case.
Conversions between lifetime and retention rate (“lifetime 1 year → Rr = 0 %”).
traps: Retention uses the customers of the **previous period** as denominator, survival the **original cohort**.
Subtract the acquisition cost **once** (month/year 1), not every period.
Apply overhead (e.g. 20 %) to revenue before subtracting CAC.
The biggest or fastest-growing segment is not necessarily the one with the highest CLV.
